utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May I invite the Court Deputy, first of all, to call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-17-S, the Prosecutor versus Miroslav Bralo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll make it clear initially that the Trial Chamber has decided that I should preside over this sentencing hearing. First of all, may I take the appearances for the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, counsel. My name is Mark Harmon. Appearing with me is Mr. Fergal Gaynor and case manager, Sebastiaan van Hooydonk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. And for the accused, Mr. Bralo.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Jonathan Cooper. I appear as counsel. With me is Ms. Virginia Lindsay, who appears as legal consultant, and Ms. Snezana Bukal, who is our investigator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper. Mr. Bralo, can you please confirm to me that you are able to hear the proceedings in a language which you are familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. The sentencing hearing this afternoon follows upon a plea of guilty tendered by the accused Miroslav Bralo on the 19th of July of this year, following which Trial Chamber I entered convictions against him on each of eight counts. I just want to summarise these counts at the outset. The first is a count of persecution as a crime against humanity, and deals with a number of episodes, including participation in the killing of the family of Osman Salkic prior to an attack on Ahmici; participation in the attack on Ahmici itself; destruction of the lower mosque at Ahmici; the forcible transfer of Muslim residents; the burning of Muslim residences in Ahmici; and the participation in the killing of 14 members of the Salkic and Cerimic families. Count 2, which is a count of murder as a violation of the laws or customs of war, involved the killing of three unarmed Muslim men near Kratine. Count 3 to 6 are related to each other and involve torture, repeated rape, and unlawful confinement of one particular Muslim woman. The various charges are of torture or inhumane treatment as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. Count 4 is torture as a violation of the laws and customs of war, and these two are closely related, 3 and 4. Count 5 involves outrage upon personal dignity, including rape, as a violation of the laws or customs of war. And Count 6 is unlawful confinement as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. Then Count 7 and 8 are related to each other. Count 7 is unlawful confinement of civilians as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. And Count 8 is inhumane treatment as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions. And these two charges involve the unlawful confinement of Muslim civilians, forcing them to dig trenches, and the use of prisoners as human shields. Now, that's an outline of the terms of the indictment and the factual basis for the Plea Agreement. Can I now move to ask the counsel here to give me an indication of how it's proposed to undertake the hearing, what course of action you propose to follow. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do not have any witnesses who will be testifying. It was my intention to merely make oral submissions to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Associated with these oral submissions, I assume you will make reference to a number of exhibits, or proposed exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a set of exhibits that essentially are the attachments to the Prosecutor's brief. Some of them consist of statements both under seal, and should be under seal, and not under seal, and there are photographs. We will tender copies of all of our attachments in the course of this hearing. It is my intention to have some of the visual images put on the monitor during the course of my remarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And do you intend that any material you actually submit in writing or in graphic form to the Chamber should have any particular status, or is it simply material in the general sense, I think, envisaged in Rule 100?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: General material, Your Honour. There are some statements, however, that should remain under seal. Those have been identified in our trial brief, in the face sheets that are in front of each of the attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are certainly statements among the papers in both briefs to which there may be existing protective measures. Are you aware of any such?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour, and that's why I have put some under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Now, Mr. Cooper, do you intend to follow a similar course?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in your case, there's the additional question of whether the accused intends to say anything further.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, that's right. My client intends to say a few words at a particular point in my address to Your Honours, if that's convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. The only question that arises in my mind over the timing of that is that I would anticipate Mr. Harmon making submissions, followed by you, and that would complete the hearing. Everything that will be referred to is already out in the open except anything that the accused, Mr. Bralo, might say. And I wondered if it might not be appropriate simply to hear from him first of all. But if that's going to disturb your plans, then obviously the Trial Chamber won't insist upon it, but would that not perhaps be a better way of proceeding?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I think that, with respect, may well be the best course. There are a number of -- forgive me. There are a number of preliminary matters that I ought to raise before the sentencing hearing proper starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before we get to these, give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think our preference, Mr. Cooper, would be to follow the last course suggested, which is to hear from Mr. Bralo first and then we can hear Mr. Harmon's submissions and then your submissions, if that's okay. Now, you mentioned preliminary matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. There are a number of preliminary matters to raise. May I say, though, that they do not affect our ability to deal today with matters for the sentence hearing. It may not be possible, however, to complete all of the matters upon which there may be factual material or there may be material upon which there should be submissions. However, I envisage that those matters can be dealt with either by written submissions or in some other format, without necessitating a return to Court. But at this stage, there are a number of outstanding matters. If I can take Your Honour through them briefly. The first issue is co-counsel. And as I embark on a short list, I wonder if at this stage it would be appropriate to go into private session, because of the nature of the matters that I'm about to refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go into private session briefly, Mr. Cooper, as briefly as possible, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Given the indications we've had of the time likely to be taken, we will adjourn now for 20 minutes. We'll resume sharp in 20 minutes, with a view to hearing from Mr. Bralo and hearing, if possible, both counsel's submissions this evening. We'll do our best to achieve that. If not, we have tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cooper, should we now hear from Mr. Bralo?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bralo, I understand that you want to make a statement, and the Trial Chamber will now hear you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see there's no person in the English booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're doing it from this booth and we just had a channel glitch. We apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you care to start again, please, Mr. Bralo.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for allowing me to address you and the public. I would like to apologise to all of the victims and to their families, their close and distant relatives, and all of those who experienced the horrors of war through me or my co-fighters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bralo. Does that complete your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please be seated. Now, Mr. Harmon, I think we would like to hear your submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, counsel. Your Honours are here today to sit in judgement on Miroslav Bralo. To put this case in the proper historical context, one must return to Central Bosnia in the spring of 1993, when the Bosnian Croats were allied with the Bosnian Muslims against their common foe, the Bosnian Serbs. The Bosnian Croats suddenly turned on their allies throughout the Lasva Valley and ethnically cleansed villages throughout that region. Overwhelmed by fear and poisoned by propaganda, peaceful villagers turned into killers and eliminated their own neighbours to further the goals set by others of ethnic separation. The goals of this murderous campaign were not set by Miroslav Bralo. He was not the architect of ethnic separation. He was not even a mid-level perpetrator. In the hierarchy of malefactors, he held a low rank, but his low rank did not prevent him from becoming notorious for his particular cruelty and deeds for their savagery and for his complete lack of mercy. Miroslav Bralo has pleaded guilty to eight counts in an amended indictment. Your Honour has summarised those counts, something I had intended to do and I'm grateful to Your Honour for doing so. I've had the privilege of appearing before this Tribunal for 11 years, and I recall participating in some of its earliest litigation, particularly in 1996, when I participated in a Rule 61 hearing involving the Karadzic and Mladic cases. Great stock was put into the fact that this Tribunal would afford an opportunity for the world to hear the voices of the victims and to allow it to reflect soberly on the meaning of their words. Nine years have passed since that hearing, and in the intervening nine years, the Tribunal has focussed on complex issues of substantive and procedural law, creating important precedents that hopefully will serve to guide future generations of international lawyers, judges, and scholars. But it seems to me in the process of grappling with many of the difficult issues that confront this Tribunal, and I do not intend this to be a criticism, our work is taken on a more impersonal and abstract quality, oddly deflecting our attention away from what actually happened to our fellow man in the time of war. War crimes are about men and women and children who were abused, murdered, and maimed, whose families were shattered and whose loved ones had been consigned to shadows and to memories. This case clearly underscores why the United Nations created a war crimes tribunal. In determining what is an appropriate sentence in this case, I submit to Your Honours that the appropriate starting point for that analysis was enunciated by the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case, wherein that Trial Chamber stated that the sentence to be imposed must reflect the inherent gravity of the criminal conduct of the accused. It is hard to imagine more grave conduct, both in terms of its nature and in terms of its scope. Miroslav Bralo's criminal conduct includes the rape and torture of a helpless woman, the destruction of an important mosque in Ahmici. And I have put that image for Your Honours and for the public on the screen. This is a mosque that was destroyed by Miroslav Bralo and a colleague. His conduct includes the participation in the extirpation of the village of Ahmici, including the burning of residences, killing, and forcibly expelling the Muslim residents from that village. I direct your attention to the next image that appears on the screen. This is an image of the house of one of the statements of a young boy we submitted, Adnan Zec. And Your Honours will notice in the foreground dead civilians. This picture was taken on the morning of the 16th of April, 1993. Miroslav Bralo's conduct also includes forcing civilians to dig trenches at dangerous front line positions and using civilians as human shields. His conduct also includes the murder of 21 civilians, 9 of whom were children. Who were Miroslav Bralo's victims? Were they faceless, nameless people whose identities are forever lost in the numbing lists of statistics that we see associated with this war? Of course not. There was the Osman Salkic family. And if we take a look at the next image, Your Honour, this image shows Osman Salkic in -- designated by the number 2. Mr. Salkic, on the evening of the 15th of April, was killed, along with his wife, who was 55 years old, and their daughter, Mirnesa, who was 29 years old. If we take a look at the next image, Your Honour, this next image in item number 1 is a picture of Mirnesa Salkic. As I say, she was 29 years old when Miroslav Bralo slit her throat. Then there's the family of Emsad and Nihada Salkic. Emsad, the patriarch, was 37 years old, and Nihada, who is shown in the next image, she is image -- figure number 3. She was 34 years old. They had three children, who were also killed. Those children, if we take a look at the next image, were Senad Salkic, who was 16 years old at the time he was killed, and Nermin Salkic, who was 10 at the time of his death. This picture is the only picture that I had available to me. It was taken some years before the actual killing. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. In addition, Your Honour, the daughter of Emsad and Nihada Salkic, Melisa Salkic, who was 8 years old at the time of her death, was also killed. There are, Your Honour, no survivors of the Emsad Salkic family or the Osman Salkic family. Next there was the family of Esad Salkic. Esad Salkic was the man who is referred to in the Defence brief, who was killed by Mr. Bralo in February of 1993. He is not the subject of this prosecution. But his family consisted of his wife. And if we could have the next image. His wife, who was Fatima Salkic, depicted in the next image. She was 32 years old at the time she was killed. Esad Salkic had three children, a son Adis, and daughters Adisa and Alisa. If we turn to the next image, Your Honour, this is an image of Adis Salkic, who was 14 years old at the time of his killing. If we turn to the next image, another child of Esad Salkic. This is Adisa Salkic. She was 11 years old at the time of her death. Their daughter, who was 2 years old at the time, Alisa, is the sole surviving member of her family. Then there was the Mehmed Cerimic family. If we turn to the next image, please. This picture was taken five years before their deaths. This shows, in number 1, the patriarch of the family, Mehmed Cerimic, who was born in 1946. It shows his wife in number 3, who was born in 1952. And it shows his three children, who at the time of their deaths were 7 years old, 17 years old, and 14 years old. There are two members of this family who survive. Then there was Fuad Kermo. If we could turn to the next image. Mr. Kermo was married, the father of two children. He was 25 years old when he was murdered by Miroslav Bralo. There was Ibrahim Pezer who was 26. We do not have an image of Mr. Pezer. And there were two men whose identities we do not know who also died at the hand of Mr. Bralo. As we contemplate this carnage, I'm reminded of the words of the poet Rupert Brooke, who spoke of young soldiers killed in the First World War. Rupert Brooke's words apply equally to Miroslav Bralo's victims. Rupert Brooke said: "These hearts were woven of human joys and cares, washed marvellously with sorrow, swift to mirth. The years had given them kindness. Dawn was theirs, and sunset, and the colours of the earth. These had seen movement, and heard music; known slumber and waking; loved; gone profoundly friended; felt quick the stir of wonder; sat alone; touched flowers and furs and cheeks. All this is ended." And indeed, Your Honour, for Miroslav Bralo's murdered victims, all this is ended. But for his living victims, it has not ended and it has not ended for 12 and a half years. In determining the proper sentence in this case, it is our submission that it is appropriate for you to consider the impact that Miroslav Bralo's crimes had on the victims and their families. In that respect, Your Honours, we have submitted numerous victim impact statements to the Trial Chamber. Three of the statements are under seal, and I shall not identify the victims by name, but I shall refer to them in general terms and to the impact that the crimes had on them in general terms. Let us then listen to the voices of some of his living victims, 12 and a half years after he committed the crimes to which he has pleaded guilty. One victim, designated as Witness C and filed under seal, whose husband was murdered by Bralo, who was personally threatened by Mr. Bralo, has written to Your Honours about the impact that the crimes had on her life and on the lives of her young children. And she wrote in her submission: "If I wrote everything I could write, a book thicker than the thickest book in the world, and whoever read the book would cry because of the sorrow and the pain I carry inside of me, if a stone could read, it would cry." Her description of the impact of Miroslav Bralo's crimes on her and her small children has been a 12 and a half year odyssey of despair, fear, and pain. Her children have suffered, she more so. She says in her letter to you: "I wash my face with tears." This victim, who was threatened by Miroslav Bralo, brandishing a bloody knife and threatening to kill her and her children, remains fearful today. Miroslav Bralo's image remains indelibly etched in her memory. She is in a poor physical and mental state as a result of Miroslav Bralo's crimes. Facts that are confirmed by a professional social worker who has worked with Witness C and her family for three and a half years. The social worker's statement has been filed under seal. Her objective analysis of the victim and the impact that the crime had on her and her family members is clear and unambiguous, and it is our submission that the impact of Miroslav Bralo's crimes on Witness C significantly exceeds that usually suffered by indirect victims of murder. Another of Miroslav Bralo's victims has, through a declaration of an Office of the Prosecutor investigator, described the impact that Miroslav Bralo's crimes had on her 12 and a half years after the events. The tableau she paints is bleak, one of enduring and inescapable suffering, permanent emotion and physical damage. It is clear that this victim dehumanised and tortured by Bralo, is permanently damaged by his conduct and has lost forever many of those qualities that make a life vibrant and emotionally rich. Another victim, Witness B, whose statement also is filed under seal, is a living victim of Bralo and of his partners in crime. She has suffered painful physical and serious psychological consequences that she attributes directly to the crimes committed by Miroslav Bralo. She has suffered, her children have suffered as well. She describes to Your Honours a journey of despair, a journey that none of us can imagine, a journey that none of us would ever want to take. If we turn to Ahmici, which is part of the persecution count, on the 15th of August, 1993, Miroslav Bralo was in prison, where he was being detained, awaiting trial for the charges relating to the killing of Esad Salkic. That killing took place in February of 1993. Miroslav Bralo was released for the purpose of participating in the attack on Ahmici that was to occur the next morning. The purpose of that attack was to ethnically cleanse Ahmici, to kill all Muslim males of military age, and others, bearing arms, to burn all Muslim residences and to forcibly expel all Muslim residents from the village. It was clearly a criminal plan, and Miroslav Bralo was a willing and enthusiastic participant in it. Regarding this attack, the Office of the Prosecutor has submitted for Your Honours' consideration a representative sample of statements from victims of that attack, in which they describe the impact that the crimes committed in Ahmici had on their lives. Their voices, Your Honours, I am confident, fairly reflects the impact of these crimes on hundreds of victims from Ahmici. If we take a look at the first statement that I'll refer to, the statement of Elvir Ahmic, Elvir Ahmic was 14 years old at the time Ahmici was attacked. He lived with his mother and his father, his 8-year-old brother, and his 4-year-old sister. On the 16th of April, in the early morning, he witnessed his younger brother murdered, his mother mortally wounded. He himself was wounded. As his mother lay dying, her words to him were, "Elvir, find your father, take care of your sister. Take the money that is left and bury us." Twelve and a half years later, Elvir, in his statement to the Trial Chamber, said, describing both his physical pain, which was caused by shrapnel and bullets that remain in his body, and his enduring emotional pain, he says, and I quote: "I do have emotional pain, and this pain will stay with me for the rest of my life. I miss my mother and brother a lot and I think of them every day. In the years that my sister and I needed our mother most, we lost her. This is one of the reasons why I simply cannot find peace of mind." Another victim. Adnan Zec. I displayed earlier, Your Honour, an image of his house that was burnt on the morning of the 16th of April. He lived in that house with his mother, his father, and his two younger sisters. As he fled from his home, he was shot and wounded, and he feigned death. And as he lay there, he saw his mother and father and two sisters running in his direction. He observed his mother and father and 11-year-old sister murdered in front of him. His 6-year-old sister miraculously survived, but Adnan Zec and his sister were left as orphans. He describes to Your Honours the impact that those crimes had on him. "The war and the killing of my parents made me, without my fault, to a kind of homeless person drifting from one place to another. One of the biggest problems for me is the missing presence of my father and his support. Prior to the conflict, my father was already planning for my future. Shortly before the conflict erupted, he wanted to open a small shop and start to build a house for me. The plan of my father was that I was to take over the store once I will be grown up. This guidance and support I missed due to the killing of my father. When I am thinking about this now, I easily get depressed and it gives me huge emotional pain. I try to push away the scenes of the killing of my family, but it is not possible to do so, in particular, the scenes of running, trying to escape, the last moments before my sister and parents got killed. I suffer sleeplessness, getting emotional, and psychological pain." Abdullah Ahmic is another victim from Ahmici. On the 16th of April, he lived in a house with his mother, father, three sisters, and a brother. His 27-year-old brother was executed, his father was executed in front of him. Abdullah Ahmic was shot in the temple. He survived, miraculously. He feigned death. His mother and three sisters, sisters were aged 24, 23 and 16, were killed the following day. Mr. Ahmic is physically disabled as a result of what happened to him. His family house was burned to the ground. He lost his entire family and he says: "We who were the victims of this war, in comparison to people who did not lose any family members, we have that additional difficulty to struggle to live with these terrible things over and over and over again, which surely does present a great burden on the whole organism. As for my personal life, I'm pretty much handicapped, having lost all of my family. Just look at the son of mine. He is here alone, having not other children to play. If my family would still be alive, this house would be full of other children." Ibnel Famic, who led religious services in the Islamic community describes the destruction of the village of Ahmici and its two mosques. And he says: "With the beginning of the conflict, the religious life of the Islamic community, as well as life generally in Ahmici, ceased to exist." Fatima Ahmic, whose son was murdered in front of his wife and small children, whose invalid husband was murdered and whose son's house was burnt to the ground has provided Your Honours with a victim impact statement. As she says: "I was going through severe emotional pain, in fact, these pains are still part of my life. Every day I close my eyes. It doesn't matter if it is day or night. I see the killing of my husband and son in front of me. I went through the worst things that could happen to one person. I have lost my closest family and all my belongings." All these things are following me since this time and they are not leaving my mind. I have to cry several times a day." Finally, I refer to the statement of Kazi Ahmic, who was 52 when Ahmici was attacked. At the time of the attack he resided with his wife, son, and nephew. On the day of the attack, as he was fleeing Ahmici with his wife, his wife was shot in the head by a sniper. She perished shortly thereafter. In another part of Ahmici, Cazim Ahmic's son and nephew were killed. During the conflict he lost more than 60 relatives. He says, and I quote: "With the attack, my life was destroyed. The images of killing of my loved ones are still in front of my eyes. On several occasions, I almost died due to my sorrow. The biggest difficulty for me is to overcome the loss of my immediate family members. I had a happy life with my wife and children, and all of a sudden someone comes and destroys all of that. Killing your loved ones and depriving you of all material wealth. You can't explain those traumas." The circles of suffering emanating from the crimes committed by Miroslav Bralo, either personally or in concert with others, have been life-altering events from which sadly many of the victims have been unable to escape. Many of his victims, through no fault of their own, have been condemned to life sentences of pain and sorrow, and it is our submission that it is proper for your consideration to consider the victim impact statements when you determine what sort of a sentence should be imposed on Miroslav Bralo. Now, in our brief, Your Honour, we have identified a number of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. factors which we submit should be considered by the Trial Chamber as factors in aggravation. The first of those is a large number of victims who were killed by Miroslav Bralo. Turning to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, I refer Your Honours to the Deronjic case. In that case, the Trial Chamber accepted the following factors to be aggravating: "The large number of civilians who were killed, subjected to the risk of being killed, forcibly displaced and deprived of their property." The crimes to which Miroslav Deronjic entered a guilty plea related to the ethnic cleansing of a small village, Muslim village, in the Bratunac municipality. It's quite similar to the attack on Ahmici. The attack on Glogova was an attack on a defenceless Muslim village that was attacked by superior Bosnian Serb forces. It was a surprise attack. In the course of the attack, Muslim homes were intentionally torched. The mosque was completely destroyed. 64 Muslim villagers perished, and the entire Muslim population from Glogova was forcibly expelled from the village, and indeed from the municipality. Miroslav Deronjic's liability was based on the fact that he ordered that attack. It was based on the fact that he participated in a joint criminal enterprise in that attack. He did not personally kill any of the 64 victims in Glogova. As I said earlier, Bralo didn't order attacks in order to separate Muslims from Croats. He didn't order the attack on Ahmici, but his hands-on role in the attack are significant. It's our submission, Your Honour, that the large number of victims in this case is a proper factor of aggravation that should enhance the sentence of Miroslav Bralo. In this case, Your Honour, as I've discussed earlier, there were 21 murder victims of Miroslav Bralo. There are also the victims in Ahmici, deaths, in our submission, which were clearly foreseeable to Mr. Bralo when he participated in this attack on Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, what was the sentence imposed in Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic received a ten-year sentence, Your Honour. I should add that Mr. Deronjic provided substantial cooperation to the Prosecutor's office. I was the Prosecutor in that case. Mr. Deronjic provided to us original documentation. He sat for a minimum, as I recall, of 11 interview sessions with the Prosecutor's office. He testified in five cases, five separate cases, publicly. Mr. Deronjic discussed two significant elements of the Srebrenica massacre, one a document that he had helped author and that had been used by the Bosnian Serb authorities to suggest -- in fact, to say that nothing had happened in Srebrenica. He acknowledged the crimes in Srebrenica at the time. The crimes in Srebrenica had been denied. Indeed, there had been a report by the -- a draft report by the Republika Srpska saying that there had been no more than 100 people killed in Srebrenica. There were other aspects of his cooperation, but the bottom line was, Your Honour, his cooperation was substantial, and it is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Testimony for the five cases would have been subsequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Testimony in the five cases would have been subsequent to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It was before. I believe it was before the sentencing. Three of the cases may have been before the sentencing. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did he plead guilty?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He pled guilty, pursuant to a Plea Agreement. And in that Plea Agreement, there was -- he received a credit of substantial cooperation from the Prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, are you familiar with the cases in which guilty pleas have been entered?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm familiar with a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In how many has the Prosecution offered substantial cooperation? Not offered, but agreed that there was substantial cooperation? Was it something that you agreed to sparingly or are you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- fairly liberal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have been involved in four plea agreements, where I have said there has been substantial cooperation. I can tell Your Honours that the first was the Erdemovic case. Mr. Erdemovic was actually involved in two cases, two agreements. I was the senior lawyer in the first case. That subsequently was reversed by the Appeals Chamber for ineffective assistance of counsel, and Mr. Erdemovic subsequently returned and entered a new Plea Agreement. But without any doubt in my mind, I was involved in that case from the day one. Mr. Erdemovic came to the custody of this Tribunal. He was immediately and volunteered immediately to discuss matters with the Prosecution. I sat with him during those discussions. His statements to us were lengthy and truthful. This was at a time, Your Honour, when Srebrenica -- when we did not have access to Srebrenica crime scenes. Mr. Erdemovic identified the locations of crime scenes, he identified participants in the execution squad of which he was a member, he identified the structure and hierarchy of his unit in the VRS. He testified, I think, in five cases, including the Rule 61 hearing, publicly against Karadzic and Mladic. That's the first case. The second case I was involved in was the Cesic case. Mr. Cesic gave a statement, a complete statement to the Prosecutor's office. We acknowledge that he had participated -- there was substantial cooperation. There was the Plavsic case. I'm missing one case, Your Honour. And the Deronjic case, which I've already discussed. So those are cases where there has been substantial cooperation that I have been involved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That you have been involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I can't say, Judge Robinson, whether all of the cases that have resulted in plea agreements have resulted in an acknowledgment of substantial cooperation by the Prosecutor's office. But I am capable fully of distinguishing between the cooperation of the defendants I've identified, that I've been personally involved with, and Mr. Bralo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I stand corrected. There was no cooperation in the Plavsic case. So let me stand corrected. My memory has faded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should have known that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he's testified in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not testify in the Milosevic case, Erdemovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I don't know the full line-up of witnesses in that case, Your Honour. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, we submit, Your Honour, that the second aggravating factor in this case is the youth of the victims. If Your Honours refer to the case of the Prosecutor versus Kunarac at all, this was a case that involved a number of rapes, the rape victims were quite young. The ages of some of those victims 12 years old, 15 years old, 15 and a half years old, 16 and a half years old, 17 years old. The Trial Chamber in that case considered the youthful age of the victims to be an aggravating factor. The Appeals Chamber affirmed that finding. Of Bralo's 21 homicide victims, nine of them were minors at the time of their deaths. The ages of the nine victims were 7 years old, that's Sanela Cerimic and Elena Salkic; 8 years old, Melisa Salkic; 10 years old, Nermin Salkic; 11 years old, Adisa Salkic; 14 years old, Elvedin Salkic, 16 years old, Adis Salkic and Senad Salkic; and 17 years old, Edin Cerimic. Another factor that we considered to be aggravating in this case relates to the exacerbated humiliation and degradation of Witness A during her rape and torture. In the Celebici case, defendant Delic was found guilty of torture by way of raping two women detainees. One of his victims was raped in the presence of his colleagues, which the Trial Chamber found exacerbated her humiliation and degradation. The Trial Chamber found in those circumstances that they were aggravating factors that played in determining Delic's sentence. In the Aleksovski case, the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber found that the commission of violent offences against vulnerable, helpless victims or persons were those placed in the situation of inferiority constitutes an aggravating circumstance. And finally, in the Furundzija case, the Trial Chamber considered that the treatment to which Witness A had been subjected to be "a particularly vicious form of torture for the purpose of aggravating the sentence imposed." Witness A in the Furundzija case is the same Witness A who Miroslav Bralo raped and tortured, as described in Counts 3 and 6 of this indictment. It is our submission that the following factors relating to the rape and torture of Witness A should be considered as aggravating factors: Repeated death threats to Witness A, her rape in front of members of the Jokers, the unit to which Miroslav Bralo was a member; her repeated rape over several hours; his biting her during the rape; his failure to release her when he was aware that she was being raped by members of the Jokers when he was in a position to release her. So those, Your Honour, are three factors in aggravation, we submit, should be considered by Your Honours in determining the sentence. Now, in face of these staggering crimes for which Miroslav Bralo has made guilty pleas, he has also made a plea for mitigation. It is important and it is fair for the Prosecution to address his submissions, and I'll do so now. It is our submission, Your Honour, that Miroslav Bralo is entitled to three factors of mitigation. The first factor is his voluntary surrender. While we're unaware of the precise circumstances surrounding the transfer of Miroslav Bralo to the Tribunal, we take the position that his voluntary surrender merits your consideration. The second factor is his guilty plea before the commencement of trial. It is also our submission that this circumstance merits your consideration, for a number of reasons. 1: It has spared witnesses from being required to come to The Hague to testify about painful and traumatic events that so disrupted their lives. The events in Central Bosnia have been the subject of five trials before this institution: The Blaskic case, the Kordic and Cerkez case, Aleksovski case, the Furundzija case, and the Kupreskic case. Mr. Bralo's guilty pleas have spared many of those victims from having to return to The Hague yet again to testify about the events in Central Bosnia. Secondly, his guilty plea has saved the resources of this institution by avoiding the expense of a potentially lengthy trial. And finally, Your Honours, his guilty plea may contribute to the process of reconciliation in Central Bosnia. To Miroslav Bralo's credit, he has accepted his responsibility for the crimes committed in Ahmici and its environs during the HVO's efforts to expel Muslims from Central Bosnia. He has acknowledged that the attack on Ahmici was an offensive operation, criminal in design and purpose, and he is the first Bosnian Croat to do so before trial. He thus stands, Your Honours, in stark contrast to other defendants and witnesses in other cases litigated in this institution who have made efforts to mislead this Court. Miroslav Bralo, to his credit, has not done so. The last factor in mitigation, Your Honour, that we submit is one that should be considered by Your Honours, is the factor of remorse. The defendant who exhibits true remorse for his actions, according to the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, is entitled to have that fact considered by the Trial Chamber. I have studied the Defence brief, which I consider excellent, and their submissions, and all of the submissions contained in it, and it appears to me that Miroslav Bralo is genuinely remorseful and has embarked on a personal voyage of reconciliation and atonement. He has also made efforts to identify the location of minefields that could continue to kill and maim people in the Lasva Valley. I don't know the results of those efforts, but his effort is worthwhile. These factors are positive factors that have led my office to the conclusion that his remorse is sincere, and it is our submission that remorse is an appropriate factor for your consideration. There is no doubt that Miroslav Bralo was a useful tool to others whose perverse agenda was to cleanse the Lasva Valley of Muslims. Miroslav Bralo enthusiastically served his masters. However, being a tool for others does not excuse conduct which, by every measure, was excessive, even when viewed through a prism distorted by war and conflict. Miroslav Bralo still must be judged by his deeds, and so we come Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to the matter of sentence. What is a fair sentence for Miroslav Bralo, who committed or who aided and abetted in the murder of 21 people, 9 of whom were children? What is a fair sentence for Miroslav Bralo, who tortured and brutally raped a defenceless woman? What is a fair sentence for Miroslav Bralo, who willingly participated in a criminal attack on a defenceless village, an attack where he killed one unarmed man, or he set fire to houses, and where he helped forcibly expel all of the Muslim villagers who survived the carnage? What is a fair sentence for a man who intentionally blew up a house of worship? What is a fair sentence for a man who uses civilians as forced labourers and human shields and who in the process gratuitously humiliated them? For the crimes that Miroslav Bralo committed, in many courts of the world, his sentence would be life; he would spend the rest of his life in prison. And in some jurisdictions he would forfeit his life. In this institution, he can be incarcerated for the rest of his life. It is our submission, Your Honour, that individually each of these crimes merits a substantial prison sentence. Collectively, they deserve more. In light of the gravity of the offences committed by Miroslav Bralo and taking into consideration the factors of mitigation that are merited in this case, it is our submission that the appropriate sentence for Miroslav Bralo is that he serve a minimum mandatory 25 years in prison before he be considered for release. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Cooper, we are going to continue with the hearing, but we're going to have a five-minute break, and there are about 40 minutes on the tape. So if you can't manage it, then we'll obviously have to accommodate you tomorrow, but I give you notice that that is the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. --- Break taken at 5.50 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I've two questions. I hadn't, prior to your submission just now, made the link between the name of the victim in respect of whose killing the accused was actually in custody before the commission of the matters we're dealing with, and the family victims of the same name who were a group of his victims. Can I take it that there's nothing sinister in that connection, that you simply mention it as a matter of fact and no more than that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's all I mention it for, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the second question relates to the sentence that you've just proposed. Is there any precedent in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal for a sentence to be a minimum period before the expiration of which it will not be possible for the accused to be released -- or to be the subject of an application for earlier release?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe there is, Your Honour. I refer Your Honours to the judgement on the sentencing appeal of Dragan Nikolic of 4 February 2005, paragraph 95, in which the Appeals Chamber said, and I quote: "Accordingly, the Appeals Chamber finds that a Trial Chamber may determine what it considers to be the minimum term of imprisonment an accused should serve." In a separate opinion, Judge Shahabuddeen says, and I quote: "There's no doubt about the availability of the power to order a minimum term of imprisonment." That's the authority that we cite, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that the first time that that had happened? Or are you not aware?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour. I'm aware of this authority. I'm more than happy to continue to research it, Your Honour, and make written submissions on the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood that, generally speaking, the regime in which the sentence was being served would be the regime that would be followed. And of course, some regimes do have the sort of provision you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that if the Court were to impose an order with a minimum mandatory sentence, then it would be incumbent on locating a regime that would honour such a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Cooper, we are properly geared up to hear you fully, so we would like now to hear your submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Well, Your Honours, might I first address the points that Your Honours have raised to Mr. Harmon. It is, of course, appropriate that there should be consistency in sentence between cases at this Tribunal which share a factual basis. As Your Honours will see from my sentencing brief that I make reference to three cases which share, in certain respects, an identical factual basis to this one. And I must say that the submissions that I have made make reference to the sentences actually passed in those cases. And I understand those cases as operating in the original framework, if I can put it like that, of a sentence which takes effect in accordance with the regime in the country in which that sentence is served. It occurs to me that if Mr. Harmon is right, then his proposed sentence would be of very much graver effect than any of the cases in the matters that I've cited, even though the headline figure may appear to be the same. For a country which gives between one third and one half of credit for good behaviour in the course of conduct of a sentence, the effect of Mr. Harmon's approach would be to propose a sentence of perhaps 40 or even 50 years. So might I start with a very substantial health warning in relation to my submissions, because I'm comparing what I invite the Court to impose, that is, in the circumstances of this case, a sentence which will have effect in accordance with the regime in which that sentence is served. That that would accord with the comparator cases which I've cited. If it is that Mr. Harmon is to propose to make additional written submissions about that matter, plainly, it would be appropriate to hear from the Defence as well. But essentially, the question of sentence is for the Trial Chamber. It's for the Trial Chamber to make an assessment of the gravity of the offending, aggravated by those matters which are properly available, and mitigated by whatever mitigation there is, no matter under which head it might fall. And I'm going to invite the Court to do no more than look at the entire picture, which includes the gravest offending, and I accept significant aggravation, but which also contains some matters which should also be taken account of in mitigation of the eventual sentence. So in terms of my submissions, I'm going to start and end by referring to my client's remorse. It's deep and long-lasting, and it is active. And I'm going to set out what I mean by those matters in the course of the submissions I make. But I have to make clear at the very outset that my client, and I, on his behalf, acknowledge the gravity of the offending of which Your Honours are now seized of. I acknowledge not only the suffering of those directly affected in 1993, but also the continuing suffering of those directly or indirectly affected in every month of every year from that date to this. Some of those matters are set out in the extremely powerful statements which have been provided as part of the Prosecution brief, which are very effecting, and this Trial Chamber will properly recognise that those are only a sample of the voices of people who were affected by Mr. Bralo's offending. The second thing that I have to acknowledge expressly on Mr. Bralo's behalf is his personal responsibility for each of the actions which have led to harm. Whatever the context, those were acts which he acknowledges were wrong, and that he always knew to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that separate from remorse?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I think, with respect, that's a component of his remorse. It's a recognition now of something which he accepts he was seeking to deny at the time. Your Honour will be aware that a handwritten statement has been provided by Mr. Bralo which sets out something of his thinking then about his offending behaviour, about his behaviour in the immediate aftermath of it, and also the journey, as Mr. Harmon has described it, which has brought him from then to now, and the realisation that it is his responsibility and that the matters that he is to be sentenced for are matters which, in reality, were matters which could never, ever have been justified, whether they were subject to orders or not, they could never, ever have been justified. And he, in carrying them out, no doubt together with others, that he was fully aware of the unlawful nature of those acts, not only unlawful, but also immoral. Might I go on by acknowledging the aggravating factors that have been relied on by the Prosecution in this case. I don't take issue with a single one of the factors that have been brought forward. As to the large number of victims, that is plainly aggravating. Your Honours are, of course, entitled to aggravate sentence to acknowledge that aggravating feature. Mr. Harmon's made reference to the Deronjic case in relation to, as he points out, a similar massacre, in which civilian men, women, and children were effectively ordered to their deaths by Mr. Deronjic and the sentence that resulted in that case. Well, plainly, many similarities apply in this case as well. Secondly, Mr. Harmon relied on the youth of the victims. And once again, I take no issue with that at all. That is a gravely aggravating feature of this case. And thirdly, the exacerbated humiliation regarding one victim in particular, Witness A. Once again, that is plainly right to take account of. Mr. Harmon also invites the Court to consider victim impact and respectfully we agree. That is entirely appropriate, and the voices from those who have been named and others who cannot be, yet others again whose statements have not been obtained, those should be listened to, and listened to as individuals as well as cumulatively. On behalf of Mr. Bralo, there's one thing to say about one of those witness statements, and that's the witness statement of Witness C, who describes a particular episode in either her house or a particular house. That episode is not one that Mr. Bralo, having thought about the matter, recognises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have it. It's Attachment B.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Certainly. It's Attachment B and it's dealt with in my friend's brief at his page 14, paragraph 62 onwards. The particular passage is set out at paragraph 63 of Mr. Harmon's brief. Indeed, it's the final sentence of that paragraph. As I say, that's an episode which the defendant does not recognise. However, I hope that the Court can properly take account of every aspect of what is said by Witness C in this case, in this way. On behalf of Mr. Bralo, there can be no doubt that Witness C has been profoundly affected by her indirect victimisation at Mr. Bralo's hands. The full extent of her statement makes extremely troubling reading, and Your Honours will know that that is further enhanced by the statement of a support worker who assists the family. And I hope the Court considers it proper to take account of what has been set out in her statement. There can be no doubt that is her reality. And if her reality is that she continues to be troubled by images and nightmares with Mr. Bralo in them, then this Trial Chamber would be remiss not to take those matters into account. So I hope, with that one exception in relation to one passage in the statement of Witness C, I can say that there can be no exception taken to any single sentence in any of the remaining statements that have been supplied in the extremely powerful documents annexed to the Prosecution brief. And these provide material which is important to be fully recognised by the Trial Chamber in passing sentence. Your Honour, in 1993, Mr. Bralo lived in Nadioci, near to Vitez. He was a young man of 25, married, a man of good character, and within the space of two or three months, the world in which he and his neighbours lived was turned irrevocably upside down. Within the space of two or three months, he had perpetrated the gravest of crimes. Mr. Harmon has referred to the background within this turbulent region at this turbulent time, and Your Honours will know that in my sentencing submissions, I've drawn attention to two particular considerations which should be considered in assessing this course of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. offending. The first of those I set out in my submissions at paragraph 47. That's the deteriorating political and military situation in Vitez. And Your Honour will see that my submissions echo and are echoed by those of Mr. Harmon, in whose own brief there is a helpful report which seeks to set out some of the immediate background, the poisoning of the airwaves with messages of hate. In particular, in the days immediately before the attack on Ahmici, specific misinformation, which was noted by international observers, at paragraph 12 of the rapporteur's report, adding greatly to the climate of fear and hatred in the area. So it is, in my submission, entirely appropriate that the Court should be aware of the context, aware of the enormous pressures placed on many people of good character and of bad character, actors and those who were passive, political and not political. It was in that context that the second matter that I draw attention to occurred, and that is the most unusual set of circumstances leading to my client's incarceration at Kaonik Prison for the period immediately up to the very eve of the attack on Ahmici. Now, the unusual circumstances derived from initially an attack on Mr. Bralo's own home, followed by an attack by him on the person he believed to be its perpetrator. Now, the Prosecution have chosen not to indict that substantive offence, but they do point out in their own sentencing brief the enormous significance of an attack upon the house of a person. And Your Honours have, in paragraph 24 of the Prosecutor's brief, a very helpful citation from an expert witness called in the Kupreskic case, specifically on the subject of the destruction of houses and what that means. The destruction of a house, but also the destruction of a home. In this particular case, the destruction of Mr. Bralo's house is independently verified, or the damage to Mr. Bralo's house and to that of his neighbours is independently verified by the investigation which was carried out entirely properly in relation to the matters from February of 1993. And that's set out, as Your Honours know, in our Appendix C2. But the fact of my client's imprisonment at this time, in February and March of 1993, in those circumstances, at that time, made him, in my submission, uniquely vulnerable to suggestion, but it goes much further, to direct orders. The fact is that a person in my client's position at that time, in those circumstances, being released in the way that he was and on the terms that he was, to come under direct orders as a participant in an attack, was in no position to be a discriminating or a critical recipient of such unlawful orders. So it is, in my submission, appropriate to consider the highly unusual personal circumstances that took Mr. Bralo to Kaonik Prison and led to his release, set against the backdrop of the increasingly turbulent and destabilised situation. Now, Your Honours will see that in the subsequent paragraphs of my brief, I set out, from paragraph 51 onwards, particular factors which I invite you to consider when coming to each of the offences for which my client takes responsibility. Of course, there is a context for every one, but I underline his personal responsibility for every action in relation to each case. The basis for the submissions I make is the agreed factual basis in this case. I refer also to mitigating features, and I should turn now to those. I've referred, at my paragraph 64, to a series of matters which I invite the Court to consider, in the balance, as matters which are mitigating in character. They are of varied weight. And I invite Your Honours to accept that every one of the matters that are proposed is capable of carrying some weight and is properly considered by the Trial Chamber. The matter of how much weight, of course, entirely for Your Honours. But I've made reference to the prior good character of the defendant, the immediate background to the offending. And at my paragraph 68, I make particular reference to the use of Bralo, the use of this defendant by his superiors. In Mr. Harmon's brief, he makes a proposition, with which I respectfully agree, that low rank, certainly low rank per se, is not to be taken as a mitigating feature. But the use that was made by this particular defendant in these particular circumstances was, in my submission, so unusual as to amount to a mitigating feature. We say that the targeted manipulation of an inferior is relevant, especially where so much of this indictment has this defendant acting under direct orders and in the immediate vicinity of a superior, and always under the implicit threat of a return to prison if he did not comply with the instructions given. Therefore, as I've set out at the conclusion of that paragraph, Mr. Bralo was used for a period in April and early May 1993 as a weapon of war. He was used to commit murders, under orders, in the context of the attack on Ahmici. He was used to commit rape, under orders, to facilitate an interrogation. And he was used to frighten people by his commander present at the trenches. Now, I've described that as being the targeted manipulation of an inferior to commit clearly criminal actions. And the circumstances in which these behaviors occurred was, in my submission, such an unusual set of circumstances that that's a matter which should properly be taken into account. I've referred also to the limited time period covered by this indictment, again in relation to those charged against others. I've referred in passing to the sheltering of others, and statements are provided from two people who are able to say that even in this time of appalling actions, that the defendant was plainly capable still of some kindness. I've referred, finally, to steps towards rehabilitation. And really, that could be considered a heading for all that follows in the submissions that I make, because every further element is at root a step towards rehabilitation, which is a voluntary step, about which the defendant also had a choice. And on his behalf, I invite consideration of those steps that he's taken. He also has personal responsibility in relation to those and is properly exercising it. So I suggest that from 1996 onwards, the overwhelming evidence from a very substantial number of witnesses, who knew this defendant, both before the war period, during it, and after it as well, demonstrates that he was a reflective and sometimes a very troubled man, albeit one who was able ultimately to make a very significant positive contribution to those with whom he lived. And I have in mind in particular the most recently filed statements in relation to his period effectively working for the assistance of the community. In the period up to the present, this defendant has done nothing to compound his crimes, and much to mitigate them. Firstly, voluntary surrender. But as Your Honours know, there is more of a story to this. Because not only did he voluntarily surrender in 2004, we set out the detail in the sentencing brief of his earlier attempted surrender in 1997 to UN forces, in which he volunteered the statement that he had killed in Ahmici and that he could no longer live with his conscience. Those words were recorded by the officer to whom he spoke, and they are available for the Court to provide a contemporaneous record of his behaviour and his words. Your Honours will know that he was not, in fact, arrested in 1997, despite his wish, and he was thereafter freed by UN forces. And his second surrender occurred within days of the unsealing of the previously sealed indictment against him in November 2004. The next element, guilty pleas, avoid trial, emotion, and experience. Well, quite clearly, Miroslav Bralo is the first of any of the Lasva Valley defendants to come to this Tribunal and plead guilty to the matters they face prior to trial. And in so doing, he makes a decisive break with a culture of excuse and denial. I've set out in my brief the cost, in terms of time, and the cost in terms of the Tribunal, of that culture of excuse and denial. But there is a bigger cost as well, and that is the individual cost to every single witness who, in five separate cases, has endured lying or untrue cross-examination on a basis later found by the Court to be wholly misleading and effectively defences based on fraud. And I say that in relation to each of the five cases which are set out in those cases -- sorry, in that paragraph. In particular, there is one witness who will be spared a further appearance in this Court, and it will be apparent that Miroslav Bralo is the first of any defendants to acknowledge directly his responsibility for offending against that woman. The next heading is guilty pleas reflect genuine remorse. And there is again rather more to this point than there might be in many cases, because Miroslav Bralo's remorse is reflected, in particular, in admitting matters in Count 1 which could not be proved against him on the basis of information available to the Prosecutor alone. I set out in full the position in paragraph 27 of my brief. But in essence, it's this: The defendant was originally charged with counts on an indictment, and from his arrival at this Court, he indicated that that was an incomplete account of his offending. He voluntarily made disclosures in relation to each element of what is now Count 1. As a result of those voluntary disclosures, offered for nothing, in exchange for nothing, volunteered simply because they were true, as a result of that, the Prosecution felt it right to amend the indictment to create a wholly new Count 1, which covered all of this offending. Some of that offending might have been proved by the Prosecutor, but, as has been set out, it's quite clear that not all of it could have been. And we've set out that, in certain respects, only a prima facie showing was available to the Prosecutor on the basis of material available. The defendant has pleaded guilty to that material anyway. And in relation to a final matter, there was no information at all about that matter, and the defendant pleads guilty again, making full admissions to that behaviour. So the defendant faced an original indictment. He acknowledged more, and he has pleaded guilty to all. The defendant has taken a step further. He has set out what is intended to be a public document at Annex A1, which acknowledges his personal responsibility for each of the crimes he's committed. He makes a personal apology for his behaviour. And as Your Honours see, he has called on others to assist the work of this Tribunal. An extract is set out at my paragraph 78.2. And since this is not yet a public document, but it will be, I'm going to ask for Your Honours' indulgence while I read out passages from that statement which is before you at my paragraph 78.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BRALO STATES THIS
utterances.text: "I wish to make a personal apology to each one of my victims who I made to suffer and to each member of every one of the families affected by my actions. I wish to say that I am truly sorry for their suffering and the suffering of their loved ones. What I said in Court last time, I really meant. I am guilty, and I deeply regret it. My apology should go further. It should be bigger than the globe." Your Honours, my client has set out in clear terms his acknowledgment of personal responsibility. He says this: "These were acts which I always knew to be wrong, which anyone would know to be wrong, and for which there really can be no excuse at all." He goes on: "Our wrongs were so terrible. I include others here - that we even clung to them and tried to justify them. I tried to be proud of my actions and to think they were the actions of a successful soldier. Today I am ashamed of all of that, ashamed of my conduct, and ashamed how I behaved." He describes, Your Honours, in that statement being present "when women and children were gunned down in front of me." He says: "At that moment, the good soldier in me was gone, silent." He states that he was not brave enough to speak out for people whose lives should have been saved. At that time, that would be the heroic act. In the final portion of this more lengthy statement, Mr. Bralo refers to and acknowledges the moral authority of this Tribunal. He says: "I would have said let people take their own course, but I do not believe it. I would say that I encourage anyone who can do so to come forward and talk to their neighbours, to talk to the Court and begin to make their peace." Your Honour will have the full text -- Your Honours already have the full text of that statement set out at Annex A1. In addition to that document, Mr. Bralo has given a detailed statement in relation to matters of interest to the Prosecutor. He has addressed questions that have been asked of him and he has, through Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Annex A2 of the sentence brief, produced a statement which is one which will be available and to which he is committed. Further, Mr. Bralo has provided the assistance to United Nations authorities, which is set out at paragraph 79 and paragraph 80, about which I hope that Your Honours will hear further within a short period. Your Honours note that this includes assistance to the mine action centre regarding the clearance of mines. And Your Honours will recall that Mr. Bralo was a member of a reconnaissance unit which was also involved in minelaying and minesweeping, and he has particular information about those matters. And indeed, I can say that he's able to provide information about areas which are not yet mine-free, and that is a significant help to those who may be affected. I go on at my paragraph 81 to refer to positive cooperation of value to the Tribunal, because Your Honours will note that at the time that Mr. Bralo attempted to surrender to UN forces in 1997, he came armed with documents that he had with him, which he was happy to disclose, which were truthful documents, and have been relied upon and accepted as truthful documents. He did in that context assist the work of the Tribunal. He also renders himself compellable to repeat the truths that are set out in his factual basis in any future proceedings to which that testimony may be relevant. I'm finally going to refer to positive cooperation, which is not simply of value to this Tribunal and its work, but it is of value to the people of Ahmici, of the area injured by his actions. I've indicated that it is a tribute to the character of those who endured and survived the events of Ahmici that that community can temper its outrage at the wound done to it with expressions of compassion and conspicuous fairness to a person even, as Mr. Bralo is, charged with the gravest of crimes. And Your Honours may be astonished to find within the papers that you will read in relation to sentence, statements of two residents of Ahmici, both of whom profoundly affected by the events of April 1993, who are yet able to find it in their hearts to consider Mr. Bralo's actions, consider his stance towards the Tribunal, and give him some respect for that stance. Your Honours will have seen the statement of Mehmed Ahmic, the president of the municipality of Ahmici, referred to in my sentence brief at paragraph 85. He stated to our investigators that he was grateful for the opportunity to have his words and the thoughts of Ahmici considered by the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we just go into private session for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Cooper.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm obliged. I was referring to the statement of Mehmed Ahmic, who expressed himself grateful for the opportunity to have his words and the thoughts of Ahmici considered by the Tribunal. He stated this: "I know that Miroslav Bralo is the first of the defendants from this area to go to The Hague in order to admit their guilt and to do so without taking us through a trial. I consider that pleading guilty and showing remorse is positive. It is a sign of some ethical position, some morality. It would be good if everyone did the same." He goes on: "I'm asked about the impact that this will have on relations in this area. I say it will have a fantastic effect. We are now 12 years after Ahmici. If five or six or seven years ago there were people like Miroslav Bralo who would say they had done this and this, and that and that happened, it now would be much better for people to live at peace with one another here and move from the hard positions against each other. They, the actors, the perpetrators, they are often the only ones who really know just what happened. It is time to clear their consciences and I'm glad that those with some decency are now telling their crimes." Your Honours will see the full text of that powerful statement. And I pause just to note that, of course, this defendant did surrender in 1997. In fact, more than eight years ago. And as Mr. Harmon has referred to his experience of 11 years at this Tribunal, plainly, that would have had a symbolic impact had his efforts to surrender been met as they perhaps should have been. And when I make that point, I refer, of course, again to the time, effort, expense of pursuing a range of Lasva Valley trials against the sullen resistance of the defendants in those cases. Your Honours, in terms of assessing sentence, my respectful submission is this: That there are powerful matters to be considered on both sides. I've acknowledged grave offending, with significant aggravating features, albeit not with that aggravating feature of superiority, which is a factor in each of the three cases that I have relied on, as guides and comparators. On the other hand, and wholly unlike each of those three other cases of Messrs. Kordic, Santic, and Furundzija, there is substantial mitigation to be considered. For a very substantial period, this defendant has done nothing to aggravate, and much to mitigate, his behaviour. The aggravation which I've accepted, the aggravating features that I've accepted, of course will have been present in their entirety in the cases of Kordic, Santic, and Furundzija. In relation to the matters of humiliation, each one of those will have been considered by the Furundzija Trial Chamber in assessing the appropriate sentence for Anto Furundzija, but there was the additional aggravation in that case of ordering the attack. In the case of Vladimir Santic, the youth of the victims was, of course, considered by the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber. But there was in his case the additional aggravation of command. And similarly, high numbers, of course, appropriate, and I expressly acknowledge it, in the case of Dario Kordic, that was also a factor, together with others. But in his case, of course, there was the express finding of the additional aggravation of being the responsible political leader, in relation to an indictment that went for a period not of just two months or so but of two years and four months, involving offending not just in the locality of Ahmici but in the entire Lasva Valley and beyond it as well. There is, in my submission, nothing in the aggravating features of this case which takes this case beyond those that I've cited. We submit, therefore, that the cases I've cited remain a firm anchor, a sound departure point for considering the present sentence. Mr. Harmon has made his submissions about sentence length. He's acknowledged a number of matters which are included in the Defence sentencing brief, and for that I am grateful to him. His sentencing -- his own sentencing brief came to a conclusion about a proposed sentence, which does not appear to have been modified in any way by the new material which he's discovered in the course of the Defence sentencing brief. And although he's made express acknowledgment of a number of factors, including the genuineness of the remorse, together with some other matters which are set out in our pleadings, it would, in my submission, be appropriate for there to have been an express acknowledgment that those matters should properly have an impact on sentence. And there might have been that acknowledgment expressed in a modification of the sentence which the Prosecution sought. But in reality, it's the Trial Chamber's view. And we would invite the Court to be aware very much of the future in deciding the appropriate sentence. The two statements that I've referred to in particular as voices from Ahmici speak really from the heart of an injured community. It's a community of which my client was a member. He was then 25. He's now 38. His stance has won him some respect. His stance has begun to enable the community to make its peace. This is an active stance, it's an ongoing stance, and in my submission, it is profoundly to be encouraged. I concluded my submissions in this way: A substantial sentence for Mr. Bralo is clearly warranted. But we submit that a sentence which reflects Mr. Bralo's self-evident and active remorse would nevertheless send a message of hope and encouragement to defendants and victims alike that this Court prizes nations of rehabilitation and reconstruction. This goes for communities and it goes for individuals. Would Your Honours forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honours. In concluding, I say simply this: By Mr. Bralo's stance, he has made a decisive break with a culture of excuse and denial. He has instead acknowledged his own personal responsibility. In my respectful submission, he has taken a brave step in acknowledging the full extent of his behaviour here. It is something of an unprecedented step. It cannot undo the wrongs of the past, but it is the best guarantor, in my submission, that wrongs of that kind will not and cannot be repeated. I'm very grateful to Your Honours for hearing my submissions. That's how I put the mitigation on behalf of this defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just for the avoidance of doubt: Both parties have submitted their material as annexes to the briefs which were presented, and it seems to me unduly bureaucratic to go through an exercise of numbering these as exhibits. So what I propose is that they are simply left in that position, that they are annexes to the briefs which we have and which we will consider. And that so far as the Prosecution brief is concerned, they're called attachments A to Q, and so far as the Defence brief is concerned, they are annexes A to D, as revised. And if you're content with that, then what we have before us are your submissions, plus these supporting documents. And we also, of course, have the statement of Mr. Bralo.

utterances.speaker: MR. COOPER
utterances.text: I'm obliged. Might I just add that the entire Defence sentencing brief was filed confidentially, and it is my intention to make a public filing as soon as I possibly can, and to ensure that the matters that I've quoted are available in public form at the earliest possible opportunity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cooper. Yes, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is satisfactory. Our filing is public, with the exception of certain attachments that should remain under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, I, on behalf of the Trial Chamber, thank both counsel for the very full and helpful submissions they've made this evening, and also for these very helpful briefs which were submitted by both. We shall reserve judgement and pronounce our determination in this case as soon as possible. The Court is now adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.
